Abstract Background  Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax is a recognized complication of pulmonary tuberculosis; however, presentation with tension physiology followed by prolonged air leak may create diagnostic and management challenges, particularly when tuberculosis is not known at presentation. Case presentation  We report a 20-year-old male with a 3 pack-year smoking history and no known prior lung disease who presented with dyspnea, left-sided pleuritic chest pain, productive cough, and constitutional symptoms. During the initial emergency assessment, unilateral chest findings raised concern for a left-sided pneumothorax. Urgent chest radiography obtained during this process showed a large left-sided pneumothorax with mediastinal shift, and emergency needle decompression was performed as a temporizing maneuver, followed directly by placement of a 28-Fr left chest tube. Persistent incomplete lung re-expansion and continuous air bubbling prompted further evaluation. Chest computed tomography revealed multiple left-sided cavitary lesions with surrounding parenchymal infiltrates, and sputum Ziehl–Neelsen staining was positive for acid-fast bacilli in three samples, supporting active cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis in the clinical and radiographic context. Standard anti-tuberculosis therapy was initiated. Despite early symptomatic improvement and substantial lung re-expansion, air leakage persisted. Because the patient maintained adequate oxygenation, controlled drainage, and no evidence of pleural sepsis or respiratory deterioration, conservative management was continued under thoracic surgical supervision with ambulatory drainage and close follow-up. The air leak resolved 61 days after hospital discharge, and the chest tube was removed without subsequent clinical recurrence. Conclusions  This case highlights that emergency decompression should not preclude continued etiologic evaluation when pneumothorax is accompanied by constitutional symptoms, incomplete lung re-expansion, persistent air leakage, or parenchymal abnormalities. ​Background Tension pneumothorax is a life-threatening presenta­ tion of pneumothorax that requires prompt recognition and urgent decompression [1]. In young patients without known lung disease, an apparently spontaneous pneumo­ thorax may initially be presumed to represent a primary event, particularly when underlying parenchymal disease is not clinically evident at presentation [1]. However, the distinction between primary and secondary spontane­ ous pneumothorax is based on the absence or presence of clinically apparent lung disease, and patients classified as having primary spontaneous pneumothorax may still harbor unrecognized underlying lung abnormalities [2]. Pulmonary tuberculosis can underlie secondary spon­ taneous pneumothorax and, in some cases, progress to tension pneumothorax [3]. This distinction is clinically important because primary and secondary spontaneous pneumothoraces differ in morbidity, mortality, rates of hypoxia at presentation, and recommended management [2].

Pneumothorax and persistent pleural air leak are rec­ ognized complications in the setting of pulmonary tuberculosis [4, 5]. However, the published literature has more often described these complications in separate or broader clinical contexts than as a single integrated pre­ sentation [3, 4]. Although persistent air leak is gener­ ally defined and managed within time-based escalation frameworks, available guidance also acknowledges lim­ ited evidence regarding the optimal timing of interven­ tion and the need for individualized decision-making [1, 5]. We report a case of tension pneumothorax as the initial presentation of active cavitary pulmonary tuber­ culosis, complicated by prolonged persistent pleural air leak despite early clinical and radiographic improvement under conservative management.

Case presentation A 20-year-old male active smoker (3 pack-years), with no known prior lung disease, presented with a two-day his­ tory of progressive dyspnea and left-sided pleuritic chest pain associated with productive cough. He also reported recent fever, weight loss, and night sweats, without a his­ tory of chronic cough or known tuberculosis contact. On admission, he was tachycardic (130 bpm), tachypneic (35 breaths/min), and hypotensive (90/50 mmHg), with an oxygen saturation of 93% on room air. Physical examina­ tion revealed marked respiratory distress with intercos­ tal retractions. Breath sounds were markedly diminished

over the left hemithorax, with absent tactile fremitus and hyperresonance to percussion, while the right lung exam­ ination was unremarkable. No jugular venous distension was observed.

During the first emergency assessment, the combi­ nation of dyspnea and unilateral chest findings raised concern for a left-sided pneumothorax, although the diagnosis was not clinically definitive at that point. The thoracic surgery team was called immediately, and an urgent chest radiograph was obtained during this pro­ cess. The radiograph demonstrated a large left-sided pneumothorax with mediastinal shift (Fig. 1), consistent with tension pneumothorax. Emergency needle decom­ pression was then performed as a temporizing maneuver to relieve tension physiology while tube thoracostomy was being prepared, followed directly by placement of a 28-Fr left chest tube connected to an underwater seal drainage system. Laboratory investigations obtained following initial stabilization demonstrated leukocyto­ sis (12,800/mm³) with neutrophilia (89%) and elevated C-reactive protein (138 mg/L), while hemoglobin, renal function, liver enzymes, and electrolytes were within reference ranges. Despite initial intervention, post-pro­ cedural imaging demonstrated incomplete lung re-expan­ sion with residual pneumothorax, left-sided interstitial infiltrates, and subcutaneous emphysema (Fig.  2), and continuous air bubbling persisted in the drainage system.

On the day after chest tube placement, and in view of the incomplete re-expansion, associated constitu­ tional symptoms, and radiographic parenchymal abnor­ malities, chest computed tomography was performed, revealing a cavitary lesion at the apex of the left upper lobe and multiple cavitary lesions in the left lower lobe, with surrounding parenchymal infiltrates and mild left pleural effusion (Fig.  3), while the right lung remained unremarkable. Approximately three days after CT imaging, micro­ biological evaluation of sputum samples demonstrated acid-fast bacilli on three Ziehl–Neelsen stains, support­ ing the diagnosis of active pulmonary tuberculosis in the clinical and radiographic context. Because the patient remained clinically stable after the initial improvement, conservative management was continued under thoracic surgical supervision. Further surgical or bronchoscopic escalation was considered as a potential option if the clinical course became unfavor­ able; however, it was deferred because the patient main­ tained adequate oxygenation on room air, had substantial radiographic re-expansion, and showed controlled drain­ age without pleural sepsis, recurrent respiratory

compromise, or other urgent indications for interven­ tion. Given this favorable early trajectory and the ability to maintain controlled drainage outside the hospital, he was discharged with ambulatory chest drainage using a portable one-way drainage bag system.

During the outpatient drainage period, clinical follow- up was maintained approximately two to three times weekly to assess clinical status, drainage function, and air-leak persistence. During follow-up, the air leak grad­ ually decreased, became intermittent, and eventually ceased. At 61 days after hospital discharge, bubbling had been absent for 24 h, the air leak was considered clini­ cally resolved, and the chest tube was removed.

After chest tube removal, clinical follow-up was main­ tained twice during the first week and then weekly for approximately three weeks. The patient remained clini­ cally well without subsequent clinical recurrence and continued anti-tuberculosis therapy to complete the standard treatment course.

Persistent air leak is generally defined as continued bubbling after 3–5 days of chest drainage and remains a recognized challenge in spontaneous pneumotho­ rax [9]. However, such time-based definitions do not by themselves determine how persistent air leak should be interpreted or managed, particularly in complex disease- specific settings where evidence remains limited [9, 10]. In active cavitary tuberculosis, ongoing parenchymal necrosis, communication with the airways, and pleural extension may all contribute to delayed closure of the air leak [11]. In the present case, the possibility of broncho­ pleural or alveolopleural communication was considered clinically because of persistent bubbling and cavitary disease. However, no direct fistulous tract was demon­ strated on CT, and bronchoscopy was not performed; therefore, the finding was described as persistent air leak rather than confirmed bronchopleural fistula. Accord­ ingly, ongoing bubbling in this setting should not be interpreted in isolation as evidence of treatment failure [6].

Contemporary management frameworks generally sup­ port early escalation of persistent air leak, particularly when the patient is fit for definitive intervention [9]. Yet this approach cannot be applied mechanically when pro­ longed air leakage occurs alongside otherwise favorable clinical recovery [9, 12]. In our patient, continued conser­ vative management was supported by rapid symptomatic improvement, adequate oxygenation on room air, sub­ stantial radiographic re-expansion of the affected lung, and controlled ongoing drainage. respiratory compromise, superimposed pleural infection, or other urgent indication for definitive intervention. This decision was made under thoracic surgical supervi­ sion, with surgical or bronchoscopic escalation reserved for an unfavorable clinical course. At the treating institu­ tion, thoracic surgical assessment and supervised chest- drainage follow-up were available, whereas advanced bronchoscopic air-leak interventions were not routinely available. The presence of active cavitary tuberculosis, with inflamed and potentially friable parenchyma, was also considered when weighing the risks and benefits of non-urgent intervention. The ability to continue super­ vised outpatient management further supported ongoing drainage and observation over immediate invasive man­ agement. In this context, leak duration alone was insuf­ ficient to define management failure or justify immediate definitive intervention [9, 13]. This should not be inter­ preted as a general recommendation to delay interven­ tion, but as an example of individualized management in a clinically improving patient.

The presence of active cavitary tuberculosis, with inflamed and potentially friable parenchyma, was also considered when weighing the risks and benefits of non-urgent intervention. The ability to continue super­ vised outpatient management further supported ongoing drainage and observation over immediate invasive man­ agement. In this context, leak duration alone was insuf­ ficient to define management failure or justify immediate definitive intervention [9, 13]. This should not be inter­ preted as a general recommendation to delay interven­ tion, but as an example of individualized management in a clinically improving patient.

present case, although they do not fully mirror its clinical sequence. In the 53-patient series by Shamaei et al., chest- tube drainage alone relieved most surgically managed patients, with a median drainage duration of 13 days, whereas some patients required open drainage or more invasive procedures because of empyema, lung destruc­ tion, or bronchopleural fistula [7]. Freixinet et al. simi­ larly reported a mean pleural drainage duration of 12.9 days, with surgical resection required in 28% of patients, mainly for persistent air leakage or recurrence [4]. In another series, Singh and Tiwari found that underwater- seal intercostal drainage was successful in most patients, with a mean drainage duration of 17.14 days, while 7.7% were referred for thoracic surgical management because of non-resolution of pneumothorax and persistent bron­ chopleural fistula [14]. Against this background, the pres­ ent case is notable for the initial presentation as tension pneumothorax in previously undiagnosed cavitary tuber­ culosis, the substantially prolonged drainage course, and eventual resolution without surgical or bronchoscopic escalation. This variability, together with the absence of a clearly defined escalation threshold for persistent air leak in disease-specific settings [9, 10, 13], supports the educational value of reporting carefully monitored con­ servative courses when decisions are guided by clinical trajectory rather than duration alone.

Limitations Tuberculosis was diagnosed on the basis of three posi­ tive sputum Ziehl–Neelsen smears in the appropriate clinical and radiographic context, without GeneXpert MTB/RIF testing, mycobacterial culture, or drug-sus­ ceptibility testing; therefore, molecular confirmation and drug-resistance assessment were not available. This limi­ tation should be considered when interpreting diagnos­ tic certainty and may reduce the generalizability of the case to settings where molecular confirmation, culture, and drug-susceptibility testing are routinely available. Air-leak assessment was qualitative and based on clini­ cal observation of bubbling in the drainage system rather than digital quantification or standardized grading. Although persistent bubbling and cavitary disease raised concern for bronchopleural or alveolopleural communi­ cation, no direct fistulous tract was demonstrated on CT and bronchoscopy was not performed. Follow-up after chest tube removal was clinical, without a follow-up chest radiograph. As a single case, these limitations preclude defining a general threshold for escalation or a standard duration for conservative management. The case should therefore be interpreted as an example of individualized management in a clinically stable patient rather than evi­ dence that prolonged air leak duration alone can be safely disregarded.

Conclusion This case highlights that previously undiagnosed active cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis may initially present as tension pneumothorax and may be complicated by prolonged persistent air leak. Pleural decompression addresses the immediate emergency, but persistent air leakage, incomplete lung re-expansion, constitutional symptoms, or parenchymal abnormalities should prompt continued etiologic evaluation. In carefully selected patients who remain clinically stable with adequate oxy­ genation, controlled drainage, lung re-expansion, and no evidence of pleural sepsis or respiratory deterioration, prolonged air leak may be interpreted within the broader clinical course rather than by duration alone. This case supports individualized, closely supervised decision- making rather than a general recommendation to delay surgical or bronchoscopic intervention.
